case20v1-val.fake.door:
Chaturang Bills and the Diwali Stock Advance

A decision case on testing demand with a fake door

1. Opening

At 7.40 on Monday 5 October 2026, Ketan Sardesai, chief product officer of Chaturang Bills, opened a spreadsheet sent at 7.30, which was ten on Sunday night in Toronto, where his data scientist had finished it. A fourteen-day experiment had closed at midnight. It asked merchants using Chaturang's billing app in Pune, Surat, Indore and Ludhiana whether they would reach for a short-term advance to buy festival stock.

The answer was not clean. Engineering would lock its next sprint on Friday 9 October, and if the advance was to be live for Diwali on Sunday 8 November, Ketan had to commit the team that week.

2. Company background

Chaturang Bills was founded in Pune in 2019 and sells a mobile app for GST invoicing, stock records and UPI payment collection to small retailers: kirana stores, chemists, hardware dealers and cloth shops. Some 3,80,000 merchants have registered. About 1,10,000 open the app in a typical month and about 90,000 pay the ₹1,499 annual subscription, which brings in roughly ₹13.5 crore a year.

The market is crowded. Khatabook, OkCredit, Vyapar and Zoho Books compete for the same shopkeeper's phone. Chaturang's advantage is its record: every invoice is a dated, GST-tagged sale. That is why Ketan's team proposed the Diwali Stock Advance, a loan of up to ₹2 lakh disbursed by a partner non-banking finance company (NBFC) under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules. The partner would underwrite and lend; Chaturang would earn 1.0 per cent of each amount disbursed.

3. The situation

Building the feature was estimated at ₹38 lakh: ₹22 lakh of engineering time, ₹9 lakh for partner integration and certification, and ₹7 lakh for legal and compliance review. Ketan had first approved a fake-door test, which advertises a feature inside the live product before it exists to see whether anyone wants it. A card reading "Diwali Stock Advance" appeared on the home screen. Tapping it did not start an application. It opened a screen saying plainly that the advance was not yet available, asking how much the merchant would want, and offering to notify them. Chaturang collected no PAN, Aadhaar or bank details, in keeping with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and promised to delete responses if the feature was never built.

The test ran from Monday 21 September to Sunday 4 October. From the 62,000 merchants who had at least twenty invoices in the previous month and six months of tenure, 20,000 were chosen at random and split in two. Arm A saw "Stock advance, up to ₹2 lakh". Arm B saw the same line plus "1.5% a month". Exhibit 1 sets out the funnel. Of the 20,000 assigned, 16,200 opened the app and saw the card. Of those, 1,544 tapped and 550 joined the waitlist: 3.4 per cent of viewers but 2.75 per cent of merchants assigned.

The team had agreed on 17 September, before anyone had costed the build, to proceed if 3.0 per cent of assigned merchants joined the waitlist. The test reached 2.75 per cent, or 550 of 20,000.

The reading was disputed from three time zones. Kruti Sapkal in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune until 1 November, pointed out that a tap is not a loan. Ketaki Shevde, the designer in Berlin, three and a half hours behind until 25 October, had written the "not yet available" screen. Keshav Sakpal, who leads customer success from Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Pune, had telephoned 30 merchants who tapped.

4. The people

Kavita Salgaonkar, vice-president of growth in Mumbai, wants to build now. She cites Arm A, where merchants tapped at "one in eight", 12.0 per cent of viewers, though the pooled figure is 9.5 per cent, about one in ten. She also quotes the 3.4 per cent of viewers who joined, and notes the test preceded festive buying. In her view the 3.0 per cent bar is arbitrary.

Kaushik Shirgaonkar, engineering lead in Bengaluru, can reach code-complete by Friday 30 October with five engineers, but the partner needs a further week to certify the integration, so the earliest live date is Friday 6 November. He doubts demand is proven.

Kruti Sapkal, the data scientist, argues that the test measured interest only, not whether merchants would accept the price, pass the credit check or borrow again.

Ketaki Shevde accepts the test but insists that no fake door take more from a merchant than a tap and an amount.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows that price mattered. Showing it cut taps from 12.0 to 7.0 per cent of viewers, yet those who still tapped were likelier to join the waitlist, 42.5 against 31.7 per cent of tappers. Exhibit 2 adds what the 550 asked for.

Exhibit 3 is Kruti's attempt to turn the test into a decision. At 1.0 per cent on an average advance of ₹1.07 lakh, each advance earns ₹1,070, so recovering ₹38 lakh takes 3,552 advances. 6. The options

Option 1: build now. Commit Kaushik's five engineers and ₹38 lakh. The upside is a live product on 6 November, two days before Diwali. The cost is the full ₹38 lakh, committed although three of four break-even cells fail (four of four on Arm B), and a month of other roadmap work.

Option 2: a concierge pilot. Build nothing in the app. Take 120 waitlisted merchants, have the partner underwrite them by hand from Chaturang's sales data, and disburse real advances of up to ₹1.2 lakh at 1.5 per cent a month from 19 October. The upside is a measured approval rate, price acceptance and repeat draw. The cost is ₹9 lakh and a readout on 20 November, after Diwali.

Option 3: stop. Accept 2.75 per cent against the 3.0 per cent bar and put the engineers on the GST filing reminders already queued. The upside is no spend; the cost is abandoning 550 merchants who asked to be told, when one pooled scenario in Exhibit 3 would have paid.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the fake door measure, and which three things that decide the economics did it leave unmeasured?
  2. Kavita quotes 12.0 per cent and 3.4 per cent. Neither measures the 3.0 per cent bar; why not, and does her case survive when the right base is used?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, which assumptions would you most want measured before committing ₹38 lakh, and why?
  4. Which option would you take on Friday, and what would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

A fake door answers one question cheaply: would users reach for this if it were there? It cannot say whether they will pay, qualify or return. Its discipline is to set the bar beforehand, compare like with like and stay honest, as Chaturang did by revealing the truth at the first tap and collecting nothing sensitive.

One defensible path is Option 2. The test missed its own bar, so Option 1 would override it, and Option 3 would discard a real signal of 550 waitlist joins. Exhibit 3 shows the decision turning on approval rate and repeat draws, and the pilot measures exactly those. Arm A cleared the bar (3.12 per cent of assigned) and Arm B did not (2.38), and a live feature would show its price. Waiting is also cheap. If each approved merchant drew one advance at Diwali, the pooled figures (1,705 waitlisted, ₹1.07 lakh) give 682 borrowers and ₹7.3 lakh of fees at 40 per cent approval, or 1,023 and ₹10.9 lakh at 60 per cent; Arm B's (1,476, ₹0.90 lakh) give about ₹5.3 and ₹8.0 lakh. Missing Diwali costs about ₹5–11 lakh on these assumptions against a ₹38 lakh build, and a ₹9 lakh pilot buys the missing numbers.

Option 1 treats a tap as demand. Option 3 treats a guessed threshold as proof.
exp40v2-val.fake.door:
Fake doors and painted doors

A door measures a click on a promise. What separates a useful one from an expensive one is a question about bases: who could have seen it, over what window, and what they were agreeing to.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 16 February 2026, Nandini Rajadhyaksha, vice-president of product at Wistaar Pay, a Bengaluru consumer payments application with 1,84,00,000 monthly actives, was looking at a dashboard that said 10.00 per cent. It was the click-through rate on a tile placed on the Accounts tab fourteen days earlier, advertising WorthBox, a goal-based savings vault the company had not built. Tapping it produced a screen saying, honestly, that the feature was not live, inviting the user to name a goal amount, showing a zero-fee line and offering to notify her when it shipped. Nothing was concealed. The build meant twenty-two engineer-months and a partner bank — a Reserve Bank of India compliance review, and a decision she could not quietly reverse.

Her analyst, Nikita Rastogi, had rebuilt the query overnight. The 10.00 per cent was an artefact: the numerator counted taps across fourteen days while the denominator came from one weekly partition of the impressions table. Measured properly the rate was 7.20 per cent. Nandini's reaction is what this page is about: she did not ask whether 7.20 was good, but what it was 7.20 per cent of.

Six weeks later, on 31 March 2026, Nitin Revankar, head of product at Wichaar Freight Cloud in Pune, read a memo about a door for WorkLane, a compliance module for the fleet platform Wichaar sells to 412 paying accounts. The headline read: 63 of 412 accounts expressed interest (15.3 per cent). Both halves were wrong, and because the errors pulled in opposite directions, correcting one would prove worse than correcting neither.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Definition. A fake door is an entry point to a capability that does not exist, placed where a real one would go and instrumented so the attempt to enter is recorded. A painted door is the subclass sitting inside a live product, where the attempt ends in a disclosure — "not built yet" — usually with an intent-capture step. The distinction is who bears the cost: a landing-page door is shown to strangers who lose nothing, a painted door to paying customers who expect what the product displays to be real.

History. The method predates software by half a century. Mail-order houses ran split-run tests in the 1920s, advertising merchandise they had not manufactured and refunding orders they could not fill — dry testing, which the United States Federal Trade Commission's Mail Order Rule of 1975 exists partly to constrain. The software vocabulary arrives through the lean-startup tradition: the smoke test, Zynga testing game concepts as short pitches before writing code, Kickstarter's industrialised pre-order. All solve one asymmetry — building is expensive, asking is cheap — so a cheap ordinal signal carries option value, provided you know what it is a signal of.

Four positions, each with the proposition it signs:

The demand-signal school. A click is a cheap ordinal signal whose job is to rank candidates. It signs: within one product surface, the rank order of door click rates predicts the rank order of eventual adoption. Not: a click rate predicts an adoption rate.

The construct-validity school. An unpriced click measures curiosity, copy and slot salience, in that order. It signs: the absolute rate of an unpriced door is uninterpretable; only differences against a matched control door are. Not: doors should not be run.

The trust-economics school. A door spends the user's belief that what the product shows is real, and the spend never appears on the dashboard that approved it. It signs: the cost of a door is a liability recognised in a later period. Not: deception of any degree is impermissible; it accepts disclosed doors.

The sell-first school. Where customers are few and each reachable by a human, the door evades a conversation you could have. It signs: in enterprise a door is rarely necessary and never sufficient. Not: doors have no enterprise use; it accepts triage.

3. Mechanics in depth: the denominator is a design decision

Expert practice begins before the door ships, with a written definition of the population that will form the denominator. This sounds procedural; it is the whole method. Of Wistaar Pay's 1,00,00,000 Android users, 20 per cent were assigned at session start to two equal cells — one taking the WorthBox door, one a placebo door in the identical slot — leaving 80,00,000 held out. The cell cascades thus over 2–15 February 2026.

Exhibit 1 — Wistaar Pay, WorthBox door cell, 2–15 February 2026. User-level, deduplicated.
StageUsers% of assigned% of rendered
A — assigned and active at least once10,00,000100.00—
B — reached the Accounts tab at least once4,20,00042.00—
C — door rendered, visible ≥ 500 ms3,50,00035.00100.00
D — tapped the door25,2002.527.20
E — completed the intent-capture step9,5760.962.74

The B → C gap of 70,000 decomposes exactly: 42,000 on builds below 7.8, where the flag defaulted off, plus 28,000 on a cached layout. No residual; no row is a total.

Three rates share the numerator 25,200: on rendered impressions 7.20 per cent, on surface reachers 6.00 per cent, on everyone assigned 2.52 per cent. The top figure is 2.86 times the bottom, and all three get called "the CTR". Only the first is a click-through rate in the sense the phrase implies, because only its denominator holds nothing but units that could physically have clicked. The second is a surface-conversion rate; the third is right only if the decision concerns shipping to the whole assigned population at the same reach.

The window must be shared

The 10.00 per cent on Nandini's dashboard is the canonical defect, and it contained no arithmetic error. Taps were summed over fourteen days; impressions came from one seven-day partition, giving 2,52,000. The quotient is exactly 10.00 per cent and exactly meaningless, because a returning user contributes taps from days she contributes no impressions; the overstatement was 1.39 times. The rule is mechanical: numerator and denominator must share a window, a unit of analysis and a deduplication rule, written down before the query runs. Wistaar's pre-registered gate was framed that way — at least 6.00 per cent on rendered impressions and 35 per cent intent capture among tappers — and the corrected 7.20 and 38.0 per cent cleared both.

The placebo door, and the floor the slot creates

The second cell is what separates expert practice. Wistaar's placebo door held the identical slot and advertised something nobody was thought to want — sharing a savings streak into a group chat. It rendered to 3,50,000 users and drew 11,550 taps, 3.30 per cent: the floor the slot creates, the share who tap a novel tile there for reasons unrelated to the proposition. WorthBox's 7.20 is 2.18 times that floor.

Exhibit 3 — WorthBox door cell against placebo door cell. Identical slot and treatment, same window.
MeasureWorthBoxPlaceboRatio
Rendered impressions (users)3,50,0003,50,0001.00
Taps25,20011,5502.18
Tap rate on rendered, %7.203.302.18

Intent rate on rendered, %2.7360.3966.91

Intent capture among tappers was 38.0 per cent for WorthBox, 12.0 per cent for the placebo. No row is a total; the ratio column divides the two cells beside it.

Exhibit 3 holds the test's most useful finding, and it is not the click rate. The doors differ by 2.18 at the tap and 6.91 at intent capture, so the second step separates a real proposition from a null one about three times as sharply. A tap costs nothing, so the slot dominates its rate; naming a goal amount costs ten seconds and a small self-disclosure, so the proposition starts to. Every increment of cost buys construct validity and loses volume — the central design parameter, and why the evidence ladder runs from click to intent to priced intent to deposit.

What the holdout is for, and the dilution correction

One confusion is worth killing: the 80,00,000-user holdout cannot supply a control click rate, because a user with no door cannot click it. It measures harm. Wistaar's metric was the share returning in days 15–28: 61.31 per cent in the WorthBox cell against 61.42 per cent in the holdout, a difference of −0.11 percentage points. Its standard error, from 0.614 × 0.386 × (1/10,00,000 + 1/80,00,000), is 0.0516 points, so the 95 per cent interval runs −0.211 to −0.009 and the detectable effect at 80 per cent power is 0.145: real, and barely resolvable.

But −0.11 points is an intention-to-treat effect spread over 10,00,000 assigned users, of whom only 3,50,000 saw the door. Under the exclusion restriction — no effect on non-renderers, which should be stated rather than assumed silently — the effect per exposed user is −0.11 × (10,00,000 / 3,50,000) = −0.31 points. The inflation factor 2.86 is the same number as the spread between the top and bottom click rates in Exhibit 1, for the same reason: both are the ratio of assigned base to rendered base. One mis-specified base propagates into everything the test produces.

The economics follow, and the interval must come with them. 0.11 per cent of 10,00,000 assigned users is 1,100; at ₹46 of contribution per retained monthly active that is ₹50,600 a month inside the cell, about ₹23,600 over the door's fourteen-day life. Annualised on the full Android base — an assumption of unchanged render rate and slot, not a measurement — the point estimate is 11,000 users and ₹60.72 lakh a year, 31.3 times the ₹1.94 lakh the door cost to build. Carrying the interval through instead gives ₹4.97 lakh to ₹116.47 lakh a year, 2.6 to 60 times the build. Both ends price a door left up indefinitely, which no door is: a fourteen-day door is cheap, a permanent one costs the same order as the feature it advertises. Precision was never the constraint: a 20 per cent relative change in the 2.736-per-cent intent rate is detectable at 80 per cent power on about 15,300 impressions per arm, on pooled variance at the midpoint of the two rates.

4. When the method applies: three testable claims

(i) The renderable population is large enough that the decision is not price-sensitive within the sampling error. Wistaar's 3,50,000 rendered impressions satisfy this overwhelmingly; Wichaar's 89 do not. It is the most useful pre-flight check in enterprise, and it is arithmetic.

(ii) A matched placebo door can go in the same slot. Without it the absolute rate has no reference point. Wistaar had slot inventory to spare; Wichaar has one Compliance page, where two novel tiles would have been conspicuous to the same 89 accounts being measured.

(iii) The promise is semantically close to what would ship. "Goal-based savings vault, zero fee, notify me" is close. "We will warn you before your filter fails", with no price named, is not close to a ₹349-a-year service — a gap that cost Winshaa ₹2.34 crore.

Where is the idea actively misleading rather than weak? When the proposition cannot be judged without use — a door for "automatic driver-document extraction" measures whether the phrase sounds appealing, which barely predicts whether a 91-per-cent-accurate extractor is useable.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product portfolios the slot is owned by a different team than the capability, so the placebo comparison needs a negotiation and usually does not happen. Mature companies keep a standing experimental slot whose floor is re-measured quarterly; the tell that a company only claims to is that nobody can state the floor. In two-sided businesses the only defensible door is paired, rendered to both sides at once with denominators per side.

In regulated contexts the door can be unlawful rather than impolite. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns name bait-and-switch and false urgency; a door that lets a user believe a feature exists is closer to that line than product teams assume. Whether a disclosed painted door falls inside those guidelines is genuinely unsettled — they do not name fake doors — and teams should expect the answer to move. The contact detail collected is also personal data gathered for a stated purpose under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which gives the waitlist a retention clock and an owner.

In hardware-plus-software situations the cost structure inverts: the software half can be withdrawn, the expectation cannot, because the customer owns the device. In AI-native products the door cannot convey the quality level that determines value; the answer is a Wizard-of-Oz test. At the organisational seam, doors are approved in product review while the trust cost lands on support and a marketing-owned brand metric — which is why companies that handle this well route doors through the review that handles pricing.

6. Three nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

  1. The denominator is chosen, not discovered. A competent practitioner runs the door and then asks for the click rate. An expert writes the eligible population into the instrumentation ticket, because once the door has shipped without a render-level impression log the correct denominator does not exist and cannot be reconstructed. Tell-tale sign: their first question about someone else's result is "who could have seen it?", the second "over what window?", and only the third the number itself.
  2. A correction to one side of a ratio is not half a correction. Wichaar's memo was wrong in both numerator and denominator, and the two errors pulled opposite ways; fixing the numerator alone turned a projection that missed by ₹17.23 lakh into one that cleared by ₹115.15 lakh. Tell-tale sign: a revised figure that moves further in the direction the author wanted. An expert re-derives both sides from the eligibility rules before accepting any revision, because a partial fix inherits the authority of a correction without the arithmetic of one.
  3. An unpriced door measures the demand curve at zero. Not a quibble about precision — a different curve. Winshaa's unpriced tile drew 22.0 per cent of rendered households and its priced re-run 9.29 per cent; but the re-run also dropped a push and moved the slot, so that fall bounds the price effect rather than estimating it — and nobody runs the clean one-variable version, which is part of the nuance. Tell-tale sign: the rate exceeds, by more than roughly a factor of three, the adoption rate of any comparable paid feature already live.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the method works as described; the real constraints are trust cost and slot inventory. In B2B and enterprise condition (i) usually kills it: with a few hundred accounts the interval on an account-level rate contains most plausible decisions, and twenty minutes on the telephone produces evidence a click cannot. On platforms only paired doors are interpretable; for hardware and AI products section 5's limits bind.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. Pre-product-market-fit there is no live product to paint a door in, so the method degenerates to the landing-page smoke test, with a worse selection problem. At scale the measurement improves and the trust cost rises. Doors are not "for startups"; cheap doors with unmeasured floors and no holdout are — and they are not cheap, merely unbilled.

8. Three worked examples

(a) Wichaar Freight Cloud — the half-correction that inverted the recommendation

The memo's two errors pulled against each other. 63 counted admin users where the account count was 41, inflating the numerator 1.54 times; 412 swept in accounts that could never render the tile, which sat behind the Pro tier and a ten-vehicle threshold, deflating the rate 4.63 times. The denominator error is larger, so the memo's 15.3 per cent understated the account-level rate by 3.01 times — which is why fixing the numerator alone did damage.

Recomputed, the lesson is sharper than a single correction. The memo's own figures project ₹65.77 lakh and miss the cost line by ₹17.23 lakh, so as written it never cleared. What produced the ₹115.15 lakh that did clear was the half-correction: an analyst replaced 63 users with 41 accounts and left the 412 denominator standing. Fixing the denominator too returns −₹2.20 lakh, and the base that matches the numerator — the 89 accounts that rendered — returns −₹40.20 lakh.

That band is the most optimistic honest frame here: it inherits column three's render-fix assumption and propagates no uncertainty in the 60-per-cent conversion, which rests on 23 purchases from 38 accounts and carries a standard error near 7.9 points. Break-even is ₹1.7874 lakh per account per year, ₹14,895 a month, 2.7 per cent above the price tested.

(b) Wistaar Pay — a door that cleared its gate and still did not authorise a build

Nandini's door passed both thresholds, and what that implied about adoption was almost nothing until one unknown was estimated. Define the attenuation factor α as paid adoption among rendered users divided by intent capture among rendered users. At full Android rollout, with the flag and cache defects fixed to a 97 per cent render rate, the rendered population would be 1,00,00,000 × 0.42 × 0.97 = 40,74,000; the placebo-net intent rate of 2.736 − 0.396 = 2.340 points gives a pool of 95,332. At ₹214 of annual contribution per adopter against ₹60.80 lakh a year of annualised cost — ₹30.80 lakh engineering, ₹6.00 lakh compliance, ₹14.40 lakh partner-bank fees, ₹9.60 lakh support — the decision reduces to one number.

Adopters = 95,332 × α; each row is a scenario, not a total. The middle row is break-even α, from 60.80 / (95,332 × 214 / 1,00,000) = 0.298. It excludes the door's running harm, since once WorthBox ships no door remains; were it kept alongside, ₹4.97 to ₹116.47 lakh a year would come off every row.

Wistaar had never shipped a feature behind a door, so it had no estimate of α, and no quantity of extra click data could produce one: that numerator is observable only after shipping something. It is the structural limit of the method.

(c) Winshaa Devices — the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Winshaa Devices of Coimbatore makes connected water purifiers; 48,000 households across 310 societies had connected units by 2025. From 1 to 21 June 2025, product lead Nivedita Raikar placed a tile called Wodex Insights promising "we will warn you ten days before your filter fails" — no price, one push to the whole base, and for fourteen days the recharge button's slot.

It rendered to 31,200 households — the 48,000 less 16,800 who did not open the application in the window — and drew 6,864 taps, 22.0 per cent, of whom 2,746 left a mobile number, 40.0 per cent. Intent capture on the rendered base was thus 2,746 of 31,200, or 8.80 per cent; but the team planned on the 22.0 per cent tap rate, multiplied by 55 per cent price acceptance, forecast 3,775 paying households and built the service in five months for ₹2.34 crore, launching November 2025 at ₹349 a year. By February 2026, ninety days on, 1,123 were paying — 3.60 per cent of the 31,200 rendered, an over-prediction of 3.36 times, and 59.7 years of payback on year-one revenue of ₹3.92 lakh.

Three further defects, all of base. The push made reaching the tile a response to a campaign, so the 31,200 counted campaign responders dressed as users. No price was shown, so 22.0 per cent sat on the demand curve at zero. And the slot: 1,180 of the 6,864 taps, 17.2 per cent, were followed within twenty seconds by a search for "recharge" — mis-taps by people hunting a moved button. The trust cost showed too: 1,936 tickets at ₹118 each, ₹2.28 lakh, and 418 households disabling notifications against 96 in the previous twenty-one days.

Recovery, over twenty-one days in April 2026 under Nivedita and Naresh Rodrigues, the head of service operations, changed the instrument rather than the forecast. The door was re-run to 9,600 households — 100 drawn at random from each of 96 societies, every one an application opener, so the 9,600 is a rendered base and not an assigned one — with the price shown, no push, a neutral slot and a ₹99 refundable deposit as the terminal action. Taps fell to 892 of the 9,600 rendered, 9.29 per cent; deposits came from 318 of the same 9,600, 3.31 per cent; and when the service shipped in August 2026, 262 of the 318 depositors took paid annual plans, 82.4 per cent. Beside the first launch: of the 6,864 that tapped the unpriced tile, 561 were paying by February 2026, 8.2 per cent; of the 2,746 that left a number, 503 were, 18.3 per cent. The remaining 562 of the 1,123 payers had never touched the door, so the tile missed half the demand — and nobody measured what the deposit door missed.

One statistical point remains: Winshaa's households are not independent, sitting inside societies that share plumbing, water and a residents' association that talks. The deposit rate of 3.3125 per cent has a binomial standard error of √(320.28 / 9,600) = 0.183 points, but that ignores clustering. Someone proposed ρ = 0.031 from a published water-utility survey — picked rather than derived, and unsupported by Winshaa's own cells.

Exhibit 11 — the design effect derived from Winshaa's own cells. 96 societies, 100 households sampled from each, so m = 100 by design; variances in pp².

No row is a total. Σx² = 1,666 is the one quantity not reproducible from the others; printing it makes the rest checkable. The design effect uses the exact identity V = (p(1 − p)/m) · DEFF; the looser V = p(1 − p)(1/m + ρ) gives ρ = 0.0101, DEFF = 2.00 — close here, a different estimator. The interval is 3.3125 ± 1.96 × 0.259, or 2.80 to 3.82 per cent; the naive one, 2.95 to 3.67, is narrower by 1.42 = √2.01.

The floor in the seventh row is the check most analyses skip, and it is why the borrowed ρ was rejected. The variance of one cluster's proportion is not ρ · p(1 − p): at cluster size 100 it cannot fall below p(1 − p)/100 = 3.2028 pp², a standard deviation of 1.79 points, however little clustering exists. A ρ of 0.031 implies a between-society standard deviation of √(3.2028 × (1 + 99 × 0.031)) = 3.61 points; Winshaa's cells give 2.54, so the derived 0.0102 is right. The check runs the other way: a society-rate SD of 1.20 points implies ρ = −0.0056, not a small effect but an impossibility — the rates would have been computed on wrong denominators. An integer check pays too: with m = 100 every count is an integer, so Σx² must be one, and a sample SD of 2.526 would need Σx² in [1,659.30, 1,659.78), where no integer lies.

9. Three failure modes, with their early warning signs

The split-window denominator. Warning sign: the rate changes when the date range changes though the door has not. Diagnostic: over what window was the impression table queried, and is it the window of the click table? Cost late: Wistaar's cost a day; inside a board paper it is a reputational event, the corrected number always being lower.

The ineligible denominator. Warning sign: the denominator is a round, familiar number nobody had to compute. Diagnostic: name the gating conditions on rendering the door, and show the count satisfying all of them. Cost late: Wichaar's cost two weeks; found after the eighteen-month commitment it is ₹1.62 crore.

The orphaned waitlist. Warning sign: the intent-capture table has rows and no owner. Diagnostic: who contacts these people, by what date, and with what if the feature is not built? Cost late: at Winshaa, 1,936 tickets and 322 excess opt-outs — ₹2.28 lakh, plus a durable loss in the channel it uses to reach its installed base.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether an unpriced door is ever decision-grade. The construct-validity position is that it is not, and Winshaa's 3.36 over-prediction is the evidence it rests on; it would be wrong if attenuation factors proved stable within a category, since a known bias is a usable one. The demand-signal position is that the absolute level was never the claim — doors rank, and ranking survives a common multiplicative bias. It would be wrong if the bias were proposition-specific, and Exhibit 3 is uncomfortable for it: a common bias would leave the tap ratio of 2.18 and the intent ratio of 6.91 equal. Most teams have the data to run that test and never do.

Whether transparency saves the measurement or destroys it. One camp holds that a painted door must disclose, both ethically and because an undisclosed one contaminates every later measurement in the product. The other holds that disclosure changes the construct: a user told "not built yet, shall we notify you?" is asked to pre-register, a different behaviour from use with its own much lower base rate. Both are right about their own claim; settling it needs a within-product comparison most compliance functions would decline to approve.

Whether the trust cost is real at measurable scale. Wistaar's holdout found a −0.11-point retention effect whose interval prices a permanently mounted door at ₹4.97 to ₹116.47 lakh a year. Against that, most painted doors produce no detectable effect, and the sceptics hold that the detectable cases are about disruption, not deception — Winshaa moved a button people needed. They would be wrong if a disclosed, well-placed door still moved retention; the believers would be wrong if Wistaar's −0.11 points were the slot churn of any new tile, which its placebo cell could have settled and did not.

Whether doors belong in enterprise at all. The sell-first position is that with 412 accounts you telephone people, and Wichaar's interval is its best evidence. The counter is that enterprise doors are triage, not measurement: Wichaar now knows which 41 accounts to call. The live question is whether triage justifies showing a paying customer a tile that does nothing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They specify the denominator in writing before the door ships, treating a missing render-level impression log as a blocker. They always buy the floor — a placebo cell, or a slot baseline from a previous quarter. They choose the lowest rung of the evidence ladder that answers the question, not the one with the most volume. And they compute the decision's sensitivity first: Wichaar's exercise was avoidable, because the 2.7 per cent break-even move and the 89-account ceiling were knowable in advance. An expert spends an hour on that and then, half the time, does not run the door.

12. The decisions

Nandini Rajadhyaksha neither approved nor killed the WorthBox build. The door had told her what it could — the proposition beats its slot's floor by 2.18 at the tap and 6.91 at intent, and the ₹23,600 the door actually cost over fourteen days is affordable where the ₹4.97 to ₹116.47 lakh a year of a permanent one is not — and the decision now turned entirely on an attenuation factor she had no estimate of, break-even being α = 0.298. She authorised a second door with a committed step: the same tile requiring a pre-authorised ₹500 first deposit, run twenty-eight days to a fresh 5 per cent cell with the placebo retained — not for precision, but for the first observation capable of bounding α from below.

Nitin Revankar killed the WorkLane module and kept the door's output. His memo made the arithmetic the argument: the three defensible framings return −₹17.23, −₹2.20 and −₹40.20 lakh a year, the only one that clears is the one with the wrong base, and the 95 per cent band on the most generous of the three — ₹62.64 to ₹98.96 lakh — straddles the ₹83.00 lakh cost line, so the test cannot decide and a 2.7 per cent price change moves the answer. He gave the 41 clicking accounts to two executives with a priced letter of intent at ₹16,500 a month and a brief to return with signatures, not opinions.

Discussion questions

1. Wistaar's placebo cell measured a tap floor but no retention floor, so the −0.11-point effect cannot be separated from the churn any new tile causes. What would you instrument instead, and what would you give up to afford it?

2. Nitin keeps the door's triage value while rejecting its measurement value. Is that coherent, when the 41 accounts were selected by the same slot and copy effects that make the rate uninterpretable?

3. The deposit door raised precision from 8.2 to 82.4 per cent, but Winshaa never measured its recall, and the 562 payers the unpriced tile missed were never tested against it. What would you measure to learn whether it is better or merely narrower, and does the answer change between a ₹2.34 crore build and a ₹20 lakh one?

13. Going deeper

Designing discovery experiments is the parent discipline and the source of the pre-registration habit: a door without a written denominator and threshold is no experiment. The four product risks places the door precisely — value risk, nothing else. Landing-page and smoke tests are the out-of-product sibling, with a worse selection problem. Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests substitute wherever quality determines value. Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits is the rung Winshaa and Nitin moved to. Prototype testing answers what the door cannot: whether the thing behind it would be useable. The evidence ladder frames all of these — each rung costs the user more and costs you volume.
case40v1-val.fake.door:
ISB · Software Product Management · Case

Dakhal Technologies: The Door on the Home Screen

One free squad, 47 working days, a target the company is ₹8.78 crore short of, and no settled answer on whether its shopkeepers want to borrow.

1. Sunday night, Aundh

At twenty to midnight on Sunday 18 October 2026, Lekhana Tipnis sat on the floor of her flat in Aundh, Pune, with a printout of her own deck in front of her. She had rewritten slide four, the recommendation, six times since Friday, and it still said nothing.

At 19:30 the next evening the board of Dakhal Technologies Private Limited would take its monthly product review. Four of those on the call would dial in from Edison, Toronto, Berlin and Singapore. The agenda had one substantive item, written by Lavesh Thombre himself: Q4 squad allocation — decision.

It meant that Dakhal's single free squad — 7.0 FTE across four cities at ₹27.00 lakh a month — would spend the rest of the year either on a working-capital credit line for India's neighbourhood chemists or on the expiry-returns feature those chemists had been asking for since June. Lekhana did not think she knew which. What she had was a proposal: put a door for the credit product on the home screen of the live app for fourteen days and count who knocked.

Dakhal had done exactly that once, in August, for the other feature. The aftermath was still in her inbox: a change-control notice from Dubai, and three letters from shopkeepers who had waited for something that never arrived. And she no longer trusted the number August had produced.

2. The company, and a decision taken in 2022

Dakhal was founded in Pune in 2018 by Thombre and a co-founder who left in 2021. Its product, Dakhal Counter, is a billing, inventory and GST-filing application for independent pharmacies and small chemist chains — the two-metre counter under a residential building in Nagpur or Thrissur. It sells in three tiers (Exhibit 1): at 30 September 2026, 15,642 subscribed stores and a ₹21.22 crore run rate.

What constrains everything today was decided in October 2022, when Dakhal won its first enterprise account: Daleel Markets LLC, a Dubai group running 212 pharmacy-and-convenience outlets in the UAE. Daleel wanted a separate, hardened build, but Dakhal had nine engineers and no appetite for two codebases, so it put Daleel on the same release train as the shops in Nagpur. Lomesh Thosar costed a split build at four engineer-years. The consequence, which nobody wrote down, is that Dakhal cannot show one tenant something it does not show every tenant.

When the contract was renewed on 24 March 2026 for three years, to 23 March 2029, Daleel's procurement team added a change-control annexure: thirty days' written notice and written approval before any change to a surface its users see, and a second breach within twelve months lets Daleel terminate on sixty days' notice. Daleel pays ₹1.56 crore a year, 7.4 per cent of the run rate.

3. The industry

India has several lakh independent chemist shops, many still on a paper day-book and more on the long-established billing packages — Marg ERP in the pharma trade, TallyPrime and Vyapar in general retail — whose users switch rarely. Above them Apollo Pharmacy, MedPlus and Wellness Forever run their own chain systems; Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Netmeds have taken a slice of prescription demand online; Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart have taken part of the over-the-counter basket.

The chemist's margin is thin, his capital sits in stock that expires, and his credit comes from his distributor — which is why everyone in this category eventually looks at lending. Khatabook and OkCredit built ledgers first; Razorpay, Paytm and PhonePe reach the same counter from payments; the UPI rails NPCI operates have made merchant cash flow legible. But lending is licensed: under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions a software company cannot originate credit on its own book, must route the loan through a regulated entity, and must not present itself to the borrower as the lender. Dakhal holds one non-binding letter of intent, from a mid-sized Mumbai NBFC, dated 29 September 2026.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

On 6 February 2026 the board set a ₹30 crore exit-rate ARR target for 31 March 2027 — against Exhibit 1, a gap of ₹8.78 crore. Between 8 June and 17 July, Loukya Thakurdesai's team ran 142 store interviews in six cities; the ranking question behind Exhibit 3, Panel A was added after the first 24, so only 118 carry it. Expiry returns — Parat — ranked first; a credit line, Bhandval, second.

The August sequence is in Figure 1. The tile sat in the Reports tab, read Parat — expiry returns. Coming soon, and opened a screen saying the feature was not built yet, with a Notify me button. Eight days in, growth added a dismissible home-screen banner pointing at it, without telling product.

On 2 September a deck circulated headlined 31% of stores tapped the Parat door — demand confirmed. On 18 September Lalasa Thite rebuilt the funnel from raw events and produced Exhibit 2. Three things in the deck were wrong. The headline had been taken as 2,314 of the 7,480 stores that opened Reports, or 30.9 per cent, when 1,086 of the tappers had used a banner shown to a larger population; over the 13,110 stores exposed to either surface the figure is 17.7 per cent. The 3,962 taps Talpade had quoted to the NBFC were events, not stores. And 290 of the 1,064 Notify me submissions came from stores canvassed in July.

On 12 October three letters reached Thakurdesai's team from stores that had taken the tile literally; one, a two-shop chemist in Nashik, had held expiry stock for two months and written off ₹1.84 lakh.

5. The people

Lekhana Tipnis, 36, VP Product, Pune. Position: fourteen days of a painted door beats ten weeks of a wrong build. Incentive: the CPO title, discussed for January, rides on the ₹30 crore number. Not saying: she signed off the August door without reading the Daleel annexure.

Lavesh Thombre, 44, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: the squad goes on Bhandval. Incentive: a bridge round he expects to open in January. Not saying: an investor told him in September that a credit line in the deck was worth more than one in production, and he found it clarifying.

Lomesh Thosar, 39, principal engineer, Bengaluru. Position: no new surface until tenant-level flagging exists — two engineers, six and a half weeks, ₹9.30 lakh. Incentive: he carried the blame for August. Not saying: a prototype flag has sat unreviewed in a branch since March, and a working one would let product ship without him.

Lalasa Thite, 31, data scientist, Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune until 1 November and ten and a half after. Position: the test resolves nothing finer than 1.8 points, so the stopping rule must be written first. Incentive: her re-analysis cost growth its headline. Not saying: she changed her session-stitching rule in September, which moves her own numbers.

Lumbini Tilve, 34, design lead, Berlin, three and a half hours behind Pune until 25 October and four and a half after. Position: a door is defensible only if the user learns on tapping that the thing does not exist. Incentive: a design system the August banner ignored. Not saying: she wrote that tile's Coming soon wording, and three of her five internal readers read it as "available next week".

Loukya Thakurdesai, 42, customer-success lead, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Pune. Position: no further painted doors. Incentive: renewal risk on Daleel, and a backlog in which expiry disputes are her largest ticket category. Not saying: two of the three October letters were drafted with help from her own executive.

Liladhar Talpade, 51, sales head, Edison, New Jersey, on Toronto's offset. Position: paint the door and take the numbers to the NBFC. Incentive: a 2026 variable on new-logo ARR and a pipeline forty per cent behind plan. Not saying: he has already shown the 3,962-tap slide to the NBFC's business head.

Lubaina Tulaskar, 38, head of risk and compliance, Mumbai. Position: the Bhandval tile and its form amount to a solicitation for a product Dakhal cannot provide, with no purpose the Digital Personal Data Protection Act would accept. Incentive: she alone signs regulatory undertakings. Not saying: she has not read the LoI.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Thirty-one per cent. Thirty-one per cent of the shops we showed it to put a finger on a feature that did not exist. If Parat gets thirty-one, Bhandval gets forty.”

Lavesh Thombre, product review, 2 September 2026

“The 3,962 is events; the client double-fired for sixteen days and the figure is 2,314 stores. The 7,480 is the Reports population, but 1,086 tappers came through a banner that 12,540 stores could see, so a combined rate needs the union, 13,110, and the rate is 17.7 per cent.”

Lalasa Thite, memo to the product review, 18 September 2026

“Spare me another slide with a percentage on it. Eight point seven eight crore divided by eleven hundred and thirty rupees a month, over twelve months, is six thousand four hundred and seventy-five stores, and we add five hundred and forty a month. That is the argument for credit and it does not need a door.”

Liladhar Talpade, email to Thombre and Tipnis, 11 October 2026

“Liladhar, ₹1,130 is the pooled average and it has 212 Dubai outlets at ₹6,132 and 4,180 Pro stores at ₹1,499 sitting inside it. New stores arrive at the Lite price. Eight point seven eight crore divided by ₹899 a month, a year of it, is 8,139 stores, not 6,475. Neither is reachable by March, which is the actual point.”

Lekhana Tipnis, reply, 11 October 2026

“The Nashik gentleman held his stock for two months. He is not a user, he is a man who believed us. And now you want to put money on the home screen.”

Loukya Thakurdesai, call with Tipnis, 14 October 2026

“A door you intend to open is a roadmap. A door you have no lender for is a pretence. The copy can carry it — not built yet, tell us if you want it — but only if the button records a wish and nothing else, and only if we write back. We did not write back in August.”

Lumbini Tilve, design review, 14 October 2026

“My note is narrow. Showing a tile is not lending. But a tile saying working capital for your counter, with a form that takes turnover and GSTIN, is a solicitation with a data collection attached.”

Lubaina Tulaskar, note to the board pack, 7 October 2026

8. The options as Lekhana sees them

Her deck laid out the four options of Exhibit 5, Panel B. What the table does not say is that A would carry Tilve's copy and no data capture, would cost ₹25.50 lakh with the flag, and would fall in the festive weeks when a chemist's cash need is loudest; that B's forty stores would be chosen by the people who want the answer to be no; that C, the only option that watches anyone borrow, does not fit the 47 days left; and that D adds no new revenue line at all.

She had written them as a choice between instruments. Reading them at midnight she noticed, without knowing what to do about it, that all four assume the scarce resource is the squad and the open question is whether shopkeepers want credit. Exhibit 6 says that on its own no-growth arithmetic the gap cannot be closed by credit at any penetration she would defend to the NBFC's credit team. Tulaskar's note implies the binding gate is a term sheet; Thosar's six and a half weeks implies it is a 2022 architecture decision. And nobody has costed the option Thakurdesai mentioned on Wednesday: charging for Parat as a paid add-on.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The review is at 19:30 IST on Monday 19 October 2026. Between that Monday and Thursday 31 December there are 54 weekdays, of which the company calendar blocks seven for festival and year-end holidays, leaving 47 working days. Dakhal held ₹14.60 crore of cash at 30 September 2026 and has burned a net ₹1.12 crore a month since July: from 1 October, about thirteen months of runway.

The Daleel annexure's clock also matters, and it runs from the notice rather than from the change: the first notice was filed on 19 August, so a second breach before 19 August 2027 lets Daleel leave on sixty days' notice. Tenant-level flagging does not exist. The only lender in the picture is a non-binding letter of intent twenty days old. Thite, on the call at ten in the morning Toronto time, has asked that the stopping rule be written down before anything ships.

At ten past midnight Lekhana's phone showed a message from Thombre, sent from Mumbai airport: Slide 4 still blank. Do you want me to take it? She put the phone face down on the printout, on the page where the four options sat in a row under a column headed what it can measure, and read that column again. Outside, the first delivery van of the week was already moving on Parihar Chowk.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the August door measure? State the population, the window and the surface for every rate in Exhibit 2.
  2. Exhibit 3's panels point opposite ways. What would you need to know about how each was produced before letting either move the decision?
  3. Dakhal has an interest form, a Notify me button and no lender. Where is the line between a demand test and a promise, and who should draw it?
  4. Option A runs and 24 per cent of exposed stores tap. What do you do, and what would you have done at 11 per cent? Write the rule before you see the number.
  5. If credit alone cannot close the ₹8.78 crore gap at any penetration a lender would underwrite — and Exhibit 6 leaves organic growth out, which would narrow it — what is the Bhandval programme for?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Tipnis do with the next 47 working days, what goes on slide four, and what does she say to a board whose chief executive has already told investors the credit line is in build?
exp20v2-val.fake.door:
Fake doors and painted doors

Testing demand for a feature inside a live product, before it exists

1. A Monday in June

On Monday, 18 May 2026, Mitali Pendse, head of product at Wavira Money, opened a planning document that engineers in Pune had been revising for a week. Wavira is a Pune-based personal-finance company whose app, WeShare, lets flatmates and couples split shared expenses. About 41,200 people open its Shared Expenses tab in a typical fortnight. The document proposed a feature that Pendse's team called Rent Auto-Split: on the first of each month, the app would calculate each flatmate's share of rent, send a payment request over UPI (the Unified Payments Interface, India's real-time bank-transfer rail), and chase anyone who had not paid.

The estimate came from Manish Pathare, the engineering lead. It needed six people (five engineers and a designer) for eleven weeks, which is 66 person-weeks. Wavira's finance team loads a person-week at roughly ₹0.9 lakh, so the build would cost about ₹59.4 lakh before a single user touched it. A lakh is 100,000 rupees. The feature would also carry a long tail of maintenance, because collecting money on behalf of strangers draws in compliance and dispute handling.

Everyone in the room believed in the idea. Pendse had heard flatmates complain about rent in six of her last eight user interviews. But eight interviews are a story, not a measurement, and she had been burned before: a "split by percentage" feature the year before had been requested by customers in every survey and used by 2 per cent of them within a quarter. The question was narrow and answerable. Would users in the live product actually reach for this if it were there? She proposed to find out for about one per cent of the cost of finding out the hard way.

2. The idea

A fake door test places the entrance to a feature in the live product, measures who tries to walk through it, and only then tells them the feature does not exist yet. A painted door is the same device under a different name: the door is painted on the wall, and it looks real until someone leans on it. Practitioners use the two terms interchangeably, and so does this page. The measured behaviour is a click, which is a cheap action, and the whole discipline lies in knowing what a cheap action can and cannot tell you.

The technique grew out of the "smoke test" landing pages of the lean-startup movement around 2009 to 2011, when founders began advertising products that did not exist to see whether anyone responded. No single inventor deserves the credit; the idea was assembled by many practitioners. What it was invented to solve is an old problem. Stated preference, meaning what people say they will do, is unreliable, and revealed preference, meaning what they do, is expensive to obtain if getting it requires building the product. A fake door buys a small piece of revealed preference at the price of a button.

A fake door measures whether people will reach for a thing, not whether they will keep it.

That sentence is the one Pendse could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib. It sets the scope in one line. A click is evidence of interest at the moment of seeing a label. It is not evidence of satisfaction, retention or willingness to pay.

3. How it actually works

Pendse's team ran the test in six steps, and three of them are usually left implicit. First, the team wrote the hypothesis and the decision rule before launching anything. The rule had two bars, tested on different quantities. Bar one: the rent door's click rate, as measured (the point estimate), must be at least 5.0 per cent of users who saw it. Bar two: the lift over a benchmark door, judged on the lower end of its 95 per cent confidence interval rather than the point estimate, must be at least 2.0 percentage points. The rule also stated what clearing both bars would buy: not the ₹59.4 lakh full build, but permission to run a thin pilot, a few weeks of hand-delivered service to waitlisted users, because a click cannot show retention or willingness to pay. The full build would be considered only after the pilot. A percentage point is a simple difference between two percentages: 7.0 per cent minus 3.0 per cent is 4.0 points. Writing the rule first matters because a number seen afterwards always looks like it supports something.

Second, the team chose a benchmark door, which is the step most often omitted. Some share of users will click any new button out of curiosity, so a raw click rate has no meaning without a reference. Wavira's benchmark was a deliberately dull door labelled "Change currency symbol". Third, the team defined eligibility: people who opened the Shared Expenses tab, on an app build able to render the button, during the test window. Of about 41,200 users who opened the tab in a typical fortnight, roughly 4,400 were on older builds that could not render the button; they were excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, because they could not have clicked, which leaves the 36,800 eligible users used below.

Fourth, the app randomly assigned each eligible visitor to one of the two doors, 50/50, and showed that person the same door on every visit. Fifth, a click opened a message written by Mrunmayi Padwal, the designer: "We're still building rent splitting. Want us to tell you when it's ready?" with a single optional button to join a waitlist. It asked for no payment details and no bank account. Sixth, the test ran for exactly 14 days, from 26 May to 8 June 2026. The window was placed so that it spans 1 June, the day rent falls due and flatmates are most likely to be arguing about it; it covers one rent date, not a full monthly cycle, and that limitation is part of what the result means. Fourteen days is also short enough that the novelty of the button is less likely to be mistaken for a trend. One consequence: a user first shown the door on 8 June had one day in which to click and one first shown on 26 May had fourteen, so each rate is clicks by the end of the window among users who saw the door at any point in it, not a rate over an identical period for every user. Because both doors were assigned the same way, the comparison between them is fair; the absolute levels are not.

Window for both doors: 26 May to 8 June 2026. Population: unique users on eligible builds who opened Shared Expenses; 41,200 opened the tab, 4,400 on older builds were excluded, and the remaining 36,800 were randomised, 18,400 per door. Users counted once however many times they clicked. The exactly even split is idealised for readability: in real data a sample-ratio check (testing the observed split against the intended 50/50) should be run and reported, since a large departure signals broken assignment.

Read the table line by line. Of 36,800 eligible users, half were assigned each door, and every one of the 18,400 per door was actually shown it, because the assignment was made at the moment of rendering. The rent door drew 1,288 unique clickers: 1,288 divided by 18,400 is 7.0 per cent. The benchmark drew 552: 552 divided by 18,400 is 3.0 per cent. The lift is 4.0 percentage points. Its sampling uncertainty comes from the two proportions: the standard error is the square root of (0.07 × 0.93 ÷ 18,400 + 0.03 × 0.97 ÷ 18,400), which is the square root of 0.0942 ÷ 18,400, or about 0.00226. Multiplying by 1.96 gives a 95 per cent confidence interval of 4.0 points plus or minus 0.44, which is 3.56 to 4.44 points. Both bars are met. Bar one is tested on the point estimate: 7.0 per cent is above 5.0 per cent. (The lower end of that rate's own interval is about 6.6 per cent, from 7.0 plus or minus 1.96 × 0.00188, so it would clear too.) Bar two is tested on the lower end of the lift, 3.56 points, which is above 2.0. Clearing both earns the pilot, not the full build.

The figure shows what the table says, with one addition: the bar is a pre-set line, not a post-hoc one. A reader should also notice what the figure cannot carry. A bar for 7.0 per cent looks the same whether it came from 1,288 of 18,400 or 7 of 100, which is why the cells are printed beside it.

Of the 1,288 clickers, 322 joined the waitlist. That is 25.0 per cent of clickers (322 ÷ 1,288) and 1.75 per cent of everyone who saw the door (322 ÷ 18,400). The two percentages answer different questions and must never be swapped. The first measures the quality of interest among the curious; the second measures the reach of strong interest across the whole audience.

The second pass: change one input

Suppose the only difference were the benchmark. Had the benchmark been a livelier door, say "Earn cashback on shared bills", and had it drawn 6.0 per cent (1,104 of 18,400), the rent door at 7.0 per cent would still clear the 5.0 per cent bar. But the lift would be 1.0 point, with a standard error of the square root of (0.0651 + 0.0564) ÷ 18,400, about 0.00257, so the interval would run from roughly 0.50 to 1.50 points. That fails the 2.0-point rule. The point estimate of 1.0 and the lower bound of 0.50 both fail bar two, so the recommendation flips from "run the pilot" to "do not fund the pilot on this evidence". Nothing about the rent door changed. This is the point of the benchmark: it separates interest in the feature from interest in clicking.

A second failure is purely about the base. Had an analyst divided 1,288 clicks by all 36,800 eligible users, the rate would have been 3.5 per cent, below the 5.0 per cent bar, and a good feature would have been killed. Half of those 36,800 were never shown the rent door, so they could not have clicked it. The denominator must contain only people who were exposed to that door in that window.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Click is not use, and use is not value

A click records the intention at the instant a label is read. It says nothing about whether the feature, once built, would be good enough to use in the second month. Every fake door result is an upper bound on adoption, not a forecast of it.

The label is the experiment

Users never see the feature, only the words describing it. Change "Rent Auto-Split" to "Never chase a flatmate again" and the click rate will move, without any change in the underlying demand for the feature. Test the wording you would use at launch, and be aware that you are then testing the pitch together with the idea.

Placement determines exposure

A door buried at the bottom of a settings page can show a low click rate simply because few people scroll that far. This is why the denominator counts users who saw the door, not users who loaded the page, and why teams log a render event rather than assuming exposure from a page load.

Waitlist and click answer different questions

A click costs one tap. Joining a waitlist costs a decision and sometimes a phone number. Where the second step is available, the ratio between the two is often more informative than either alone, though the waitlist introduces its own self-selection.

It is not a concierge test and not a prototype test

A concierge test delivers the service by hand to a few customers; a prototype test lets users try an approximation. A fake door delivers nothing. It is the weakest evidence of the three for value, and the cheapest for demand. Confusing it with the other two leads teams to claim more than they measured.

Novelty decays

New buttons attract attention for days. A 14-day window that spans one rent date is a compromise: it does not show how interest varies across a full month, but a one-day test would have measured the novelty and little else.

Ethics is a design constraint, not a footnote

Deceiving users, even briefly, imposes a cost on them. Three practices keep the cost small: reveal the truth immediately on click; never ask for money, credentials or sensitive data behind a fake door; and avoid features users would depend on for something urgent. In a finance product, a door implying money will move is much less tolerable than a door for a new colour theme. Regulators and trust both take a dim view of the other kind.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In a consumer product like WeShare, traffic is abundant, so a fortnight yields tens of thousands of exposures and the statistics are rarely the constraint; the constraint is how much goodwill each deception consumes. In B2B software, the same test often yields a few hundred exposures, so a clickthrough rate has wide error bars, and a fake door is better read as a way of identifying which accounts clicked and then calling them. The unit also changes: one click by one user inside a company that has 200 seats is not demand from 200 people. In a marketplace, a fake door has to be run on both sides, and a door that excites buyers about a feature sellers will not supply produces a false positive. Early-stage companies rarely have traffic for a statistically clean test and should lean on qualitative follow-up with each clicker. Large companies have the opposite problem: abundant traffic, and a brand with trust to protect, so they run the test on small slices and write the honest message with legal review.

7. Common mistakes

The wrong denominator

Symptom: a click rate that looks oddly low, or oddly high, and that no one can reproduce from the dashboard. Misunderstanding: the rate was divided by whoever was easiest to count, such as total visitors, including people never shown the door, or sessions rather than unique users. Diagnostic: for the numerator and denominator, ask whether each unit was eligible, exposed and measured in the same window. If the answer to any of the three is no, rebuild the rate.

No benchmark

Symptom: a team celebrates a "12 per cent click rate" that no one can interpret. Misunderstanding: raw clickthrough carries meaning on its own. Diagnostic: ask what a dull door would have scored. If no one knows, the result cannot be read.

Moving the bar afterwards

Symptom: the success threshold quietly appears in a document after the data, usually at whatever the result happened to be. Misunderstanding: the threshold is a conclusion rather than a commitment. Diagnostic: check the time stamp of the decision rule against the launch.

Treating a click as a purchase

Symptom: a revenue forecast multiplying clickers by a price. Misunderstanding: intention at the label equals willingness to pay. Diagnostic: ask what the user was asked to give up. If the answer is "one tap", the figure measures curiosity-plus-interest, not value.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision takes roughly this form. Before launch, the team writes a one-page note: hypothesis, door label, benchmark, eligibility, window, decision rule and the honest message. An analyst who is not on the feature team confirms that the render event fires and that assignment is random. The test runs for its 14 days and nobody looks at interim click rates in order to stop early. The results are posted as a table showing every cell: exposed users, clickers, rate, lift and interval, per door. The note says what the data cannot show. The decision follows in a meeting that lasts less than an hour, because the rule was already agreed.

9. Closing

On 10 June, Pendse presented the table. The rent door cleared both bars, and she took the result to her leadership team with its limits attached. The rule had been agreed in advance and was followed, not overridden: it had promised a pilot, not the full build, and she asked for exactly that. She did not ask for the ₹59.4 lakh build. She asked for a thin version, a single flat with manual reminders, delivered by hand to a sample of the 322 waitlisters over four weeks, at a cost of about three person-weeks (₹2.7 lakh). Her reasoning was that the door had answered one question, whether people would reach for it, and left open the others that mattered more: whether they would keep using it, and whether the payment-collection risk was acceptable. Spending under one twentieth of the budget (₹2.7 lakh against ₹59.4 lakh, about 4.5 per cent) on the second question before committing the full budget made sense.

To go further, study how to design discovery experiments more generally, since a fake door is one instrument among several, and read about concierge and prototype tests, which supply the evidence of value that a click cannot.

Two questions to sit with. If your door had scored 4.9 per cent against a bar of 5.0 per cent, what exactly would you have been entitled to conclude, and what would you refuse to conclude? And which feature in your own product would you be unwilling to test with a fake door because of what the honest message would have to say?
